title: The Guide for the Perplexed
hookLine: written for a student torn between philosophy and faith

cards: A student packs his bags and leaves his teacher. He's bright, he loves the Torah, and he's been studying logic, astronomy and philosophy. And the two are pulling him apart.
The verses say God walks in a garden, sits on a throne, smells the smoke of an offering. His philosophy says God can't have a body. Does he give up the books, or give up the reasoning?
His teacher, far away now, decides to write for him and send the chapters as they're finished. Those chapters became a book.

teach.b: Moreh Nevukhim. The Guide for the Perplexed, by Maimonides. First, the student.
The book opens with a letter to a student named Joseph. Joseph came to study with him, Maimonides writes, quick and eager, and when they were separated he decided to write for him.
Sometimes a book begins as one person worrying about another. Second, the reader. The Guide, he says plainly, is not for beginners or the general public.

teach.h: FOR THE FAITHFUL WHO ARE TORN.
teach.b: It is for a faithful, observant person who has also studied philosophy and now finds the plain sense of certain verses troubling.
That person is perplexed: follow reason and seem to abandon the Torah, or hold the Torah and feel reason has been thrown away. The book is meant to show a road that keeps both. Third, the method.

Much of the opening part goes word by word through terms the Bible uses for God, words like place, standing, seeing, coming down, and shows how each can carry a figurative meaning. Fourth, the warning.
He wrote some parts on purpose so that not everything lies on the surface.
A reader has to work, compare chapters and pay attention, and he asks readers not to explain the book to others hastily. This is not a book you skim.
It's a conversation with a teacher who expects you to think, and over the next days we'll open it a chapter at a time.

how: Some Jews study the Guide for the Perplexed slowly, chapter by chapter, with a teacher or a study partner, in study halls, universities and adult classes.

games.q: you're Joseph. the Torah says God walks in a garden and sits on a throne; your philosophy says God has no body. what does your teacher's book offer?
games.why: the Guide is written for exactly this reader: faithful, and perplexed, looking for a way to hold both.

practice: Let one thing come up that genuinely perplexes you, about faith, your life or the world, where two things you hold pull against each other, and name it in one sentence.
Then name both sides: this is what I hold, and this is what I also hold. Let them sit there together without choosing; the Guide was written for exactly this place.
